questions.q: Before deploying to Sepolia, what does this lesson say about the wallet you should use?
options: A dedicated testnet-only wallet, funded from a public faucet — never a wallet that has ever held real funds
Your personal mainnet wallet, since testnets are completely isolated anyway
Any wallet works equally well; the choice doesn't matter
A wallet borrowed from a classmate
questions.explain: The pre-deploy checklist is explicit: use a dedicated testnet-only wallet funded from a faucet, and never reuse a wallet that has ever held real funds.

questions.q: How does Hardhat 3 handle secrets like SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and SEPOLIA_PRIVATE_KEY, per this lesson?
options: Through hardhat keystore, an encrypted local store, read in config via configVariable — not a plaintext .env file
By hardcoding them directly into hardhat.config.ts
By emailing them to the deployment service
Hardhat has no mechanism for secrets at all
questions.explain: The lesson shows configVariable() pulling secrets from Hardhat's encrypted keystore (set via hardhat keystore set), explicitly replacing the older plaintext .env approach.

questions.q: In the Hardhat Ignition deployment module shown, in what order are the contracts deployed, and why?
options: Both TeachingToken contracts first, then SimplePool, because the pool's constructor needs their addresses
SimplePool first, then the tokens, in no particular order
All three contracts deploy simultaneously with no dependency order
Only the pool is deployed; the tokens are assumed to already exist
questions.explain: m.contract("SimplePool", [tokenA, tokenB]) depends on tokenA and tokenB already being deployed, so Ignition deploys both TeachingToken contracts first and the pool after.

questions.q: What does contract verification (via hardhat verify) actually accomplish, per this lesson?
options: It publishes the contract's source code so the block explorer can match it to the deployed bytecode, rather than leaving the address as just a bytecode blob
It guarantees the contract has no bugs
It automatically fixes any security issues the code has
It is purely cosmetic and has no real purpose
questions.explain: The lesson explains verification as publishing source code so the explorer can match it to on-chain bytecode, which is what makes a deployed address actually useful for someone else to inspect and trust.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what makes a project's README genuinely 'complete' for a portfolio reviewer?
options: A reviewer can understand what was built, why specific choices were made, and what's simplified — without needing to ask the author in person
The README only needs to say 'it works' with no further detail
The README should list every single git commit made
The README is optional as long as the code compiles
questions.explain: The lesson ties back to Lesson 1's portfolio strategy: a README is complete when it lets a reviewer understand the project's architecture, tradeoffs, and limitations on its own, without a live explanation from the author.
